title: Calibration weights for RL code
allegory: Probe environments are calibration weights for your RL code: a weight known to be exactly 1 kg must read 1 kg, and a ladder of weights that each test one more part of the scale tells you which part is broken.
map: a weight known to be exactly 1 kg
Probe1: one action, constant observation [0.0], one step, reward +1

chapters.name: A flat reward curve
chapters.note: reward: flat. buffer? target? γ? loss sign?

cap.1: Your learning agent isn't learning, and the reward chart is flat. The bug could be anywhere, and a real environment gives no clue which part is broken.
cap.2: RL code fails silently: a wrong discount, a frozen target network or a flipped loss sign can all produce the same flat CartPole curve.
cap.3: In a real environment the correct value function is unknown, so there is no reference to diff against. Errors in different components look identical from outside.

cap.1: A shopkeeper checks a scale with a weight known to be exactly 1 kg. If it doesn't read 1 kg, the scale is broken, whatever you meant to weigh.
cap.2: A probe environment is so tiny you know the right answer in advance. Probe 1: one action, a constant observation, one step, reward +1, so the value must be exactly 1.0.
cap.3: Probe1's correct value function is a single number, V = 1.0. Any deviation localises the bug to the update rule rather than the environment or exploration.

cap.1: Each rung adds one new ingredient. Climb until something reads wrong: the rung that fails names the broken part.
cap.2: ARENA gives a ladder of five probes: one state and one reward, then observation-dependent reward, then discounting, then action-dependent reward, then mapping what it sees to the right action. The first probe to fail points at the bug.
cap.3: Each probe isolates a mechanism: value regression, conditioning on observations, bootstrapped targets with γ, and action selection. Only then run CartPole.

cap.1: In the simplest probe the game ends right after the reward, so the right answer is just the reward: 1. No guessing about the future is involved.
cap.2: DQN's target is r + γ(1 - done)·max Q(s'). In Probe 1, done is true after one step, so the target is exactly 1.0 and the estimate should reach it within a few hundred steps.
cap.3: Ignore the done mask and the target bootstraps off an identical next observation: Q = 1 + γQ, so it converges to 1/(1-γ) instead of 1. A subtle masking bug becomes a wrong number.

chapters.name: Reading the failure

left.title: a probe fails
lines: loss near 0, value flat and wrong: frozen target
best action's log-prob falls: loss sign

chapters.verdict: Each symptom points at one part. That is the whole point of the ladder.

cap.1: Each way of failing points at a different broken part, like a mechanic who knows which rattle means which loose bolt.
cap.2: Loss near zero but the value stuck and wrong: the target network never syncs. The known-best action's log-probability falling: your policy-gradient loss sign is flipped.
cap.3: Probes pass but CartPole fails: suspect terminated-versus-truncated handling in the buffer. A probe value of 1/(1-γ) instead of 1 means the done mask is ignored.

chapters.name: Why it matters
items: Test on a known answer first
Add one ingredient at a time
Plant a known answer for interp and evals

cap.1: The single most useful RL debugging habit: check your code on problems whose answers you already know, before trusting it on ones you don't.
cap.2: Build the probes once and run them after every change. They take seconds, while a CartPole run can hide a bug for an hour.
cap.3: The principle transfers to interpretability and evals: validate a method on a planted, known answer before believing what it tells you about a real model.

caption.1: Probe 1 must learn a value of exactly 1. Slide the learning rate and watch the estimate climb to 1. Then switch on the bug and watch it sail past.
caption.2: With the done mask ignored, the target bootstraps off the identical next observation, so the estimate heads to 1/(1-γ) instead of 1. A known answer turns the bug into a wrong number.

where_else: Unit tests with known outputs, in any codebase
Checking a policy-gradient loss sign: the known-best action's log-probability must rise
Interpretability methods validated on planted features or toy models before real ones
Evals checked against a case with a known answer before being trusted on new ones

hamming.what: Tiny hand-made environments whose correct value function you know in advance, run before the real task.
hamming.when: Before training on a real environment, and again after every change to your RL code.
hamming.why: RL bugs fail silently; a known answer turns 'the reward curve is flat' into 'this component is wrong'.

object.title: The calibration ladder
object.subtitle: Tiny test worlds from simplest to real, with one tube for your one codebase running through them all.

cap.1: A ladder of tiny test worlds, smallest first, with the real task at the end. The tube is your one codebase, run through every rung.
cap.2: Probes ordered by how many mechanisms they exercise, then the real environment.
cap.3: Each block adds exactly one mechanism, so a failure is attributable to the newest one.

cap.1: The first rung: one state, one action, one step, +1. The right value is exactly 1.0, so any other number means a bug in the update.
cap.2: Probe1's value must converge to 1.0 within a few hundred steps.
cap.3: No bootstrapping and no exploration: only the regression towards r is exercised.

cap.1: Each rung adds one ingredient: then the observation matters, then the reward arrives later, then the action matters.
cap.2: Observation-dependent reward tests conditioning; delayed reward tests γ and bootstrapping; action-dependent reward tests action selection.
cap.3: A delayed-reward probe is where a frozen target network or a wrong γ first shows up as a wrong number.

cap.1: Climb until a rung fails; that rung names the broken part. Only when every rung passes is CartPole worth your time.
cap.2: If all probes pass and CartPole fails, the core update is fine: look at environment-specific plumbing.
cap.3: A passing ladder moves suspicion to what probes do not exercise, such as terminated-versus-truncated handling.

predict.q: Probe 1 pays +1 and ends after one step. What must the learned value be?

predict.q: Every probe passes but CartPole still fails. Where next?

predict.why: Probes exercise the core update; a passing ladder moves suspicion to environment-specific plumbing.
